claim: Doxorubicin is used extensively for chemotherapy of diverse types of cancer.
source: Doxorubicin is used extensively for chemotherapy of diverse types of cancer, yet the mechanism through which it inhibits proliferation of cancer cells remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical practice presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: The mechanism through which doxorubicin inhibits proliferation of cancer cells remains unclear.
source: Doxorubicin is used extensively for chemotherapy of diverse types of cancer, yet the mechanism through which it inhibits proliferation of cancer cells remains unclear.
evidence: This represents the knowledge gap that motivates the study, based on existing literature.

claim: Doxorubicin stimulates de novo synthesis of ceramide.
source: Here we report that doxorubicin stimulates de novo synthesis of ceramide, which in turn activates CREB3L1, a transcription factor synthesized as a membrane-bound precursor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B demonstrating increased ceramide synthesis upon doxorubicin treatment.

claim: Ceramide activates CREB3L1.
source: Here we report that doxorubicin stimulates de novo synthesis of ceramide, which in turn activates CREB3L1, a transcription factor synthesized as a membrane-bound precursor.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7E showing that C6-ceramide treatment stimulates CREB3L1 cleavage.

claim: CREB3L1 is a transcription factor synthesized as a membrane-bound precursor.
source: Here we report that doxorubicin stimulates de novo synthesis of ceramide, which in turn activates CREB3L1, a transcription factor synthesized as a membrane-bound precursor.
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 1A and references to prior work (Omori et al., 2002).

claim: Doxorubicin stimulates proteolytic cleavage of CREB3L1 by Site-1 Protease and Site-2 Protease.
source: Doxorubicin stimulates proteolytic cleavage of CREB3L1 by Site-1 Protease and Site-2 Protease, allowing the NH2-terminal domain of CREB3L1 to enter the nucleus where it activates transcription of genes encoding inhibitors of the cell cycle, including p21.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 1D showing that cleavage is abolished in S1P and S2P deficient cells.

claim: The NH2-terminal domain of CREB3L1 enters the nucleus after proteolytic cleavage.
source: Doxorubicin stimulates proteolytic cleavage of CREB3L1 by Site-1 Protease and Site-2 Protease, allowing the NH2-terminal domain of CREB3L1 to enter the nucleus where it activates transcription of genes encoding inhibitors of the cell cycle, including p21.
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1B demonstrating nuclear accumulation of cleaved CREB3L1.

claim: Nuclear CREB3L1 activates transcription of genes encoding inhibitors of the cell cycle, including p21.
source: Doxorubicin stimulates proteolytic cleavage of CREB3L1 by Site-1 Protease and Site-2 Protease, allowing the NH2-terminal domain of CREB3L1 to enter the nucleus where it activates transcription of genes encoding inhibitors of the cell cycle, including p21.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B showing p21 mRNA induction by doxorubicin that is blunted in CREB3L1 knockdown cells.

claim: Knockdown of CREB3L1 mRNA in human hepatoma Huh7 cells conferred increased resistance to doxorubicin.
source: Knockdown of CREB3L1 mRNA in human hepatoma Huh7 cells and immortalized human fibroblast SV589 cells conferred increased resistance to doxorubicin, whereas overexpression of CREB3L1 in human breast cancer MCF-7 cells markedly enhanced the sensitivity of these cells to doxorubicin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell proliferation data in Figure 3A showing reduced growth inhibition in Huh7-shCREB3L1 cells.

claim: Knockdown of CREB3L1 mRNA in immortalized human fibroblast SV589 cells conferred increased resistance to doxorubicin.
source: Knockdown of CREB3L1 mRNA in human hepatoma Huh7 cells and immortalized human fibroblast SV589 cells conferred increased resistance to doxorubicin, whereas overexpression of CREB3L1 in human breast cancer MCF-7 cells markedly enhanced the sensitivity of these cells to doxorubicin.
evidence: This is shown by data in Figure 4D demonstrating increased resistance in SV589 cells transfected with CREB3L1 siRNA.

claim: Overexpression of CREB3L1 in human breast cancer MCF-7 cells markedly enhanced the sensitivity of these cells to doxorubicin.
source: Knockdown of CREB3L1 mRNA in human hepatoma Huh7 cells and immortalized human fibroblast SV589 cells conferred increased resistance to doxorubicin, whereas overexpression of CREB3L1 in human breast cancer MCF-7 cells markedly enhanced the sensitivity of these cells to doxorubicin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 4F showing dramatically reduced IC50 values in MCF7/pCREB3L1 cells.

claim: Measurement of CREB3L1 expression may be a useful biomarker in identifying cancer cells sensitive to doxorubicin.
source: These results suggest that measurement of CREB3L1 expression may be a useful biomarker in identifying cancer cells sensitive to doxorubicin.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the correlation between CREB3L1 expression and doxorubicin sensitivity shown in Figures 4A-B.

claim: Doxorubicin (Adriamycin) is used widely to treat diverse types of cancer.
source: Doxorubicin (Adriamycin) is used widely to treat diverse types of cancer, yet its effectiveness is hampered by the existence of drug-resistant cancer cells.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about doxorubicin's clinical use.

claim: The effectiveness of doxorubicin is hampered by the existence of drug-resistant cancer cells.
source: Doxorubicin (Adriamycin) is used widely to treat diverse types of cancer, yet its effectiveness is hampered by the existence of drug-resistant cancer cells.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about doxorubicin resistance.

claim: The reason for drug resistance to doxorubicin is unclear mainly because the mechanism through which doxorubicin inhibits proliferation of cancer cells is not completely understood.
source: The reason for drug resistance is unclear mainly because the mechanism through which doxorubicin inhibits proliferation of cancer cells is not completely understood.
evidence: This is a logical inference connecting incomplete mechanistic understanding to unclear resistance mechanisms.

claim: Doxorubicin has been proposed to exert its cytostatic action through intercalation into DNA and production of free radicals (Gewirtz, 1999).
source: Doxorubicin has been proposed to exert its cytostatic action through intercalation into DNA and production of free radicals (Gewirtz, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Gewirtz, 1999).

claim: The mechanisms of DNA intercalation and free radical production are unlikely to be clinically relevant as the concentration of doxorubicin required to produce these effects is much higher than that achievable in patients (Gewirtz, 1999).
source: However, these mechanisms are unlikely to be clinically relevant as the concentration of doxorubicin required to produce these effects is much higher than that achievable in patients (Gewirtz, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Gewirtz, 1999).

claim: Inhibition of topoisomerase II by doxorubicin at clinically achievable concentrations leads to DNA breaks.
source: Inhibition of topoisomerase II by doxorubicin at clinically achievable concentrations leads to DNA breaks, but a consistent relationship between DNA strand breaks and the cytostatic action of the drug has not been demonstrated (Gewirtz, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Gewirtz, 1999).

claim: A consistent relationship between DNA strand breaks and the cytostatic action of doxorubicin has not been demonstrated (Gewirtz, 1999).
source: Inhibition of topoisomerase II by doxorubicin at clinically achievable concentrations leads to DNA breaks, but a consistent relationship between DNA strand breaks and the cytostatic action of the drug has not been demonstrated (Gewirtz, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Gewirtz, 1999).

claim: Doxorubicin induces renal fibrosis in mice by stimulating production of collagen (Lee and Harris, 2011).
source: In addition to blocking cell proliferation, doxorubicin induces renal fibrosis in mice by stimulating production of collagen (Lee and Harris, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Lee and Harris, 2011).

claim: CREB3L1 can activate both cell proliferation blockage and collagen expression (Denard et al., 2011).
source: The dual ability of doxorubicin to block cell proliferation and to induce collagen expression caught our attention inasmuch as we recently showed that both responses can be activated by a transcription factor called cAMP response element-binding protein 3-like 1 (CREB3L1, also known as OASIS) (Denard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Denard et al., 2011).

claim: CREB3L1 belongs to a family of transcription factors synthesized as transmembrane precursors (Omori et al., 2002).
source: CREB3L1 belongs to a family of transcription factors synthesized as transmembrane precursors (Omori et al., 2002) and activated through a process designated as Regulated Intramembrane Proteolysis (RIP) (Brown et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Omori et al., 2002).

claim: CREB3L1 is activated through a process designated as Regulated Intramembrane Proteolysis (RIP) (Brown et al., 2000).
source: CREB3L1 belongs to a family of transcription factors synthesized as transmembrane precursors (Omori et al., 2002) and activated through a process designated as Regulated Intramembrane Proteolysis (RIP) (Brown et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Brown et al., 2000).

claim: The transcription factor domain of CREB3L1 is located in the NH2-terminal 374-amino acids that project into the cytosol.
source: The transcription factor domain of CREB3L1 is located in the NH2-terminal 374-amino acids that project into the cytosol (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 1A.

claim: The COOH-terminal domain of CREB3L1 consists of 124 amino acids that project into the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The COOH-terminal domain of 124 amino acids projects into the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 1A.

claim: Viral infection triggers the RIP of CREB3L1, which undergoes two sequential cleavages mediated by Site-1 protease (S1P) and Site-2 protease (S2P) (Denard et al., 2011).
source: Viral infection triggers the RIP of CREB3L1, which undergoes two sequential cleavages mediated by Site-1 protease (S1P) and Site-2 protease (S2P) (Denard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Denard et al., 2011).

claim: The S1P-catalyzed cleavage at the luminal side is a prerequisite for the S2P-catalyzed intramembrane cleavage that releases the NH2-terminal domain of CREB3L1 from membranes.
source: The S1P-catalyzed cleavage at the luminal side is a prerequisite for the S2P-catalyzed intramembrane cleavage that releases the NH2-terminal domain of the protein from membranes, allowing it to drive transcription of genes that suppress cell proliferation such as p21 (Denard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Denard et al., 2011) and demonstrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Nuclear CREB3L1 drives transcription of genes that suppress cell proliferation such as p21 (Denard et al., 2011).
source: The S1P-catalyzed cleavage at the luminal side is a prerequisite for the S2P-catalyzed intramembrane cleavage that releases the NH2-terminal domain of the protein from membranes, allowing it to drive transcription of genes that suppress cell proliferation such as p21 (Denard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Denard et al., 2011) and data in Figure 2B.

claim: Nuclear CREB3L1 activates genes required for assembly of the collagen matrix, including collagen 1α1 (Denard et al., 2011).
source: Nuclear CREB3L1 also activates genes required for assembly of the collagen matrix, including collagen 1α1 (Denard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Denard et al., 2011) and data in Figure 2A.

claim: In the absence of doxorubicin, CREB3L1 existed as the full length precursor (∼80 kDa) in membranes and the cleaved nuclear form of CREB3L1 (∼55 kDa) was barely detectable.
source: In the absence of doxorubicin, CREB3L1 existed as the full length precursor (∼80 kDa) in membranes and the cleaved nuclear form of CREB3L1 (∼55 kDa) was barely detectable (Figure 1B, lane 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1B, lane 1.

claim: Treatment with doxorubicin markedly raised the amount of the nuclear form of CREB3L1.
source: Treatment with doxorubicin markedly raised the amount of the nuclear form of CREB3L1 (Figure 1B, lane 2).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1B, lane 2.

claim: The amount of membrane protein calnexin and nuclear protein lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) was not altered by doxorubicin treatment.
source: The amount of membrane protein calnexin and nuclear protein lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) was not altered by doxorubicin treatment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1B serving as loading controls.

claim: Nuclear CREB3L1 degradation is carried out by proteasomes (Murakami et al., 2009).
source: Doxorubicin may increase the amount of nuclear CREB3L1 through stimulation of CREB3L1 precursor cleavage or inhibition of nuclear CREB3L1 degradation, which was reported to be carried out by proteasomes (Murakami et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Murakami et al., 2009).

claim: The amount of transfected nuclear form of CREB3L1 was not affected by doxorubicin.
source: The amount of transfected nuclear form of CREB3L1 was not affected by doxorubicin (Figure 1C, lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1C, lanes 2 and 3.

claim: The amount of transfected nuclear CREB3L1 was increased in cells treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132.
source: However, this amount was increased in cells treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 1C, lanes 5 and 6), suggesting that overexpression of the transfected protein did not overwhelm the machinery that degrades nuclear CREB3L1.
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1C, lanes 5 and 6.

claim: Doxorubicin does not stabilize nuclear CREB3L1.
source: These results suggest that doxorubicin does not stabilize nuclear CREB3L1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 1C showing no effect of doxorubicin on transfected nuclear CREB3L1.

claim: Doxorubicin appears to increase nuclear CREB3L1 by stimulating proteolysis of its precursor.
source: Thus, doxorubicin appears to increase nuclear CREB3L1 by stimulating proteolysis of its precursor.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: In wild type CHO cells, doxorubicin stimulated cleavage of CREB3L1 to produce the nuclear form.
source: In wild type CHO cells, doxorubicin stimulated cleavage of CREB3L1 to produce the nuclear form (Figure 1D, lane 2).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1D, lane 2.

claim: Doxorubicin failed to produce the nuclear form of CREB3L1 in mutant cells deficient in either S1P or S2P.
source: In contrast, doxorubicin failed to produce the nuclear form of CREB3L1 in mutant cells deficient in either S1P or S2P (Figure 1D, lanes 4 and 6).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1D, lanes 4 and 6.

claim: In wild type CHO cells, a cleaved fragment with a molecular weight similar to that of the nuclear form was detected in the membrane fraction.
source: In wild type CHO cells, we also detected in the membrane fraction a cleaved fragment with a molecular weight similar to that of the nuclear form (Figure 1D, lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1D, lanes 1 and 2.

claim: The membrane-bound fragment was absent in cells deficient in S1P.
source: This fragment was absent in cells deficient in S1P (Figure 1D, lanes 3 and 4) but dramatically elevated in cells deficient in S2P (Figure 1D, lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1D, lanes 3 and 4.

claim: The membrane-bound fragment was dramatically elevated in cells deficient in S2P.
source: This fragment was absent in cells deficient in S1P (Figure 1D, lanes 3 and 4) but dramatically elevated in cells deficient in S2P (Figure 1D, lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1D, lanes 5 and 6.

claim: The membrane-bound fragment is the intermediate form of CREB3L1 that was cleaved by S1P but not by S2P.
source: These findings suggest that this membrane-bound fragment is the intermediate form of CREB3L1 that was cleaved by S1P but not by S2P.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of fragment accumulation in S1P and S2P deficient cells shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Similar cleavage intermediates were observed in earlier studies of SREBP-2 in mutant CHO cells deficient in S2P (Rawson et al., 1997; Ye et al., 2000).
source: Similar cleavage intermediates were observed in earlier studies of SREBP-2, a prototypes of RIP substrates, in mutant CHO cells deficient in S2P (Rawson et al., 1997; Ye et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Rawson et al., 1997; Ye et al., 2000).

claim: SREBP-2 was cleaved in sterol-depleted CHO cells to activate genes required for cholesterol synthesis and uptake (Brown and Goldstein, 2009).
source: SREBP-2 was cleaved in sterol-depleted CHO cells (Figure 1E, lane 1) to activate genes required for cholesterol synthesis and uptake (Brown and Goldstein, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Brown and Goldstein, 2009) and shown in Figure 1E, lane 1.

claim: SREBP-2 cleavage was not activated by doxorubicin.
source: However, this cleavage was not activated by doxorubicin (Figure 1E, lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1E, lanes 4 and 5.

claim: Doxorubicin appears to specifically induce proteolytic activation of CREB3L1.
source: Thus, doxorubicin appears to specifically induce proteolytic activation of CREB3L1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that doxorubicin activates CREB3L1 but not SREBP-2 cleavage.

claim: In Huh7 cells transfected with a control shRNA (Huh7-shControl), doxorubicin induced the expression of collagen 1α1 and p21.
source: In Huh7 cells transfected with a control shRNA (Huh7-shControl), doxorubicin induced the expression of collagen 1α1 and p21 (Figure 2A,B), both of which were shown to be direct targets of CREB3L1 (Murakami et al., 2009; Denard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown by RT-QPCR data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Collagen 1α1 and p21 are direct targets of CREB3L1 (Murakami et al., 2009; Denard et al., 2011).
source: In Huh7 cells transfected with a control shRNA (Huh7-shControl), doxorubicin induced the expression of collagen 1α1 and p21 (Figure 2A,B), both of which were shown to be direct targets of CREB3L1 (Murakami et al., 2009; Denard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Murakami et al., 2009; Denard et al., 2011).

claim: In Huh7 cells stably transfected with a shRNA targeting CREB3L1 (Huh7-shCREB3L1), induction of collagen 1α1 and p21 by doxorubicin was markedly blunted.
source: In Huh7 cells stably transfected with a shRNA targeting CREB3L1 (Huh7-shCREB3L1) (Denard et al., 2011) in which expression of CREB3L1 was drastically reduced (Figure 2C), induction of these genes was markedly blunted (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is shown by RT-QPCR data in Figures 2A and 2B comparing Huh7-shControl and Huh7-shCREB3L1 cells.

claim: For both untransfected Huh7 cells and those transfected with the control shRNA (Huh7-shControl), doxorubicin completely blocked their proliferation at a concentration between 50 and 150 nM.
source: For both untransfected Huh7 cells and those transfected with the control shRNA (Huh7-shControl), doxorubicin completely blocked their proliferation at a concentration between 50 and 150 nM (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figure 3A.

claim: The concentration of doxorubicin (50-150 nM) that blocked proliferation also resulted in maximal cleavage of CREB3L1 in Huh7 cells.
source: This concentration of doxorubicin also resulted in maximal cleavage of CREB3L1 in Huh7 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 3B.

claim: For Huh7-shCREB3L1 cells, doxorubicin at concentrations up to 500 nM failed to block their proliferation.
source: For Huh7-shCREB3L1 cells, doxorubicin at concentrations up to 500 nM failed to block their proliferation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figure 3A.

claim: Concentrations of doxorubicin up to 500 nM were not enough to trigger apoptosis of Huh7 cells.
source: These concentrations of doxorubicin were not enough to trigger apoptosis of Huh7 cells, which became apparent only when the cells were treated with 5 µM of the compound (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by TUNEL assay data in Figure 3C.

claim: Apoptosis of Huh7 cells became apparent only when the cells were treated with 5 µM doxorubicin.
source: These concentrations of doxorubicin were not enough to trigger apoptosis of Huh7 cells, which became apparent only when the cells were treated with 5 µM of the compound (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by TUNEL assay data in Figure 3C.

claim: Transfection with two distinct siRNA targeting CREB3L1 knocked down CREB3L1 mRNA by more than 90%.
source: Transfection with these siRNA knocked down CREB3L1 mRNA by more than 90% (Figure 3D), and the treatment also rendered Huh7 cells more resistant to doxorubicin (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by RT-QPCR data in Figure 3D.

claim: Transfection with siRNA targeting CREB3L1 rendered Huh7 cells more resistant to doxorubicin.
source: Transfection with these siRNA knocked down CREB3L1 mRNA by more than 90% (Figure 3D), and the treatment also rendered Huh7 cells more resistant to doxorubicin (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figure 3E.

claim: Compared to Huh7 cells, expression of CREB3L1 was higher in SV589 cells and lower in MCF-7 cells.
source: Compared to Huh7 cells, expression of CREB3L1 was higher in SV589 cells and lower in MCF-7 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by RT-QPCR data in Figure 4A.

claim: The sensitivity of the cells to growth inhibition by doxorubicin followed the order of CREB3L1 expression.
source: The sensitivity of the cells to growth inhibition by doxorubicin followed the order of CREB3L1 expression (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by comparing CREB3L1 expression levels in Figure 4A with doxorubicin sensitivity in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of CREB3L1 by two duplexes of siRNA targeting different regions of CREB3L1 in SV589 cells made them more resistant to doxorubicin.
source: Similar to Huh7 cells, knockdown of CREB3L1 by two duplexes of siRNA targeting different regions of CREB3L1 in SV589 cells (Figure 4C) made them more resistant to doxorubicin (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown by RT-QPCR data in Figure 4C and cell proliferation data in Figure 4D.

claim: The eightfold overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7/pCREB3L1(L) cells lowered the IC50 for doxorubicin from 500 nM to 10 nM.
source: The eightfold overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7/pCREB3L1(L) cells lowered the IC50 for doxorubicin from 500 nM to 10 nM, and the 300-fold overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7/pCREB3L1(H) cells further reduced the IC50 to ∼1 nM (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figure 4F.

claim: The 300-fold overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7/pCREB3L1(H) cells reduced the IC50 for doxorubicin to ∼1 nM.
source: The eightfold overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7/pCREB3L1(L) cells lowered the IC50 for doxorubicin from 500 nM to 10 nM, and the 300-fold overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7/pCREB3L1(H) cells further reduced the IC50 to ∼1 nM (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figure 4F.

claim: Treatment with 15 nM doxorubicin for 6 days did not affect proliferation of MCF-7 cells.
source: This treatment did not affect proliferation of MCF-7 cells, but markedly blocked proliferation of MCF7/pCREB3L1(H) cells, as determined by direct cell counting (Figure 4G) and by measurement of cellular DNA content (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is shown by cell counting data in Figure 4G and DNA content measurement in Figure 4H.

claim: Treatment with 15 nM doxorubicin for 6 days markedly blocked proliferation of MCF7/pCREB3L1(H) cells.
source: This treatment did not affect proliferation of MCF-7 cells, but markedly blocked proliferation of MCF7/pCREB3L1(H) cells, as determined by direct cell counting (Figure 4G) and by measurement of cellular DNA content (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is shown by cell counting data in Figure 4G and DNA content measurement in Figure 4H.

claim: CREB3L1 expression level is a key determinant of cellular sensitivity to doxorubicin.
source: Thus, CREB3L1 expression level is a key determinant of cellular sensitivity to doxorubicin.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between CREB3L1 expression and doxorubicin sensitivity shown in Figure 4.

claim: Doxorubicin induced appearance of histone γH2AX, a marker for DNA breaks.
source: Doxorubicin induced appearance of histone γH2AX, a marker for DNA breaks (Figure 5A, lane 2).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 5A, lane 2.

claim: The induction of γH2AX by doxorubicin was unaffected by knockdown of CREB3L1 expression.
source: However, this effect was unaffected by knockdown of CREB3L1 expression (Figure 5A, lane 5).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 5A, lane 5.

claim: Cleavage of CREB3L1 does not lead to doxorubicin-induced DNA breaks.
source: This result suggests that cleavage of CREB3L1 does not lead to doxorubicin-induced DNA breaks.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CREB3L1 knockdown does not affect γH2AX induction.

claim: Etoposide failed to induce cleavage of CREB3L1.
source: Unlike doxorubicin, etoposide failed to induce cleavage of CREB3L1 (Figure 5B, lane 3), even though etoposide was as effective as doxorubicin in causing DNA breaks (Figure 5A, lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 5B, lane 3.

claim: Etoposide was as effective as doxorubicin in causing DNA breaks.
source: Unlike doxorubicin, etoposide failed to induce cleavage of CREB3L1 (Figure 5B, lane 3), even though etoposide was as effective as doxorubicin in causing DNA breaks (Figure 5A, lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 5A, lanes 2 and 3.

claim: Knockdown of CREB3L1 in Huh7 cells did not increase their resistance to etoposide.
source: Accordingly, knockdown of CREB3L1 in Huh7 cells did not increase their resistance to etoposide (Figure 5C), and overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7 cells also did not increase their sensitivity to the compound (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figure 5C.

claim: Overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7 cells did not increase their sensitivity to etoposide.
source: Accordingly, knockdown of CREB3L1 in Huh7 cells did not increase their resistance to etoposide (Figure 5C), and overexpression of CREB3L1 in MCF7 cells also did not increase their sensitivity to the compound (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figure 5D.

claim: Induction of CREB3L1 cleavage by doxorubicin is not related to its inhibitory activity towards topoisomerase.
source: These results suggest that induction of CREB3L1 cleavage by doxorubicin is not related to its inhibitory activity towards topoisomerase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that etoposide, another topoisomerase inhibitor, does not induce CREB3L1 cleavage.

claim: CREB3L1 was not required for bleomycin or paclitaxel to inhibit cell growth.
source: Besides etoposide, CREB3L1 was also not required for bleomycin or paclitaxel to inhibit cell growth, an observation suggesting that CREB3L1 may be specifically involved in doxorubicin-induced suppression of cell proliferation (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figures 5E-G.

claim: CREB3L1 may be specifically involved in doxorubicin-induced suppression of cell proliferation.
source: Besides etoposide, CREB3L1 was also not required for bleomycin or paclitaxel to inhibit cell growth, an observation suggesting that CREB3L1 may be specifically involved in doxorubicin-induced suppression of cell proliferation (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CREB3L1 is not required for other chemotherapeutic drugs to inhibit cell growth.

claim: Doxorubicin and daunorubicin were reported to induce de novo synthesis of ceramide (Bose et al., 1995; Liu et al., 2008).
source: Doxorubicin and daunorubicin, a chemotherapeutic drug derived from doxorubicin, were reported to induce de novo synthesis of ceramide (Bose et al., 1995; Liu et al., 2008), a class of lipid known to inhibit cell proliferation (Ogretmen and Hannun, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Bose et al., 1995; Liu et al., 2008).

claim: Ceramide is a class of lipid known to inhibit cell proliferation (Ogretmen and Hannun, 2004).
source: Doxorubicin and daunorubicin, a chemotherapeutic drug derived from doxorubicin, were reported to induce de novo synthesis of ceramide (Bose et al., 1995; Liu et al., 2008), a class of lipid known to inhibit cell proliferation (Ogretmen and Hannun, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Ogretmen and Hannun, 2004).

claim: De novo synthesis of ceramide is initiated with the condensation of palmitate and serine (Gault et al., 2010).
source: De novo synthesis of ceramide is initiated with the condensation of palmitate and serine (Gault et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Gault et al., 2010).

claim: The rate-limiting step in de novo synthesis of ceramide is catalyzed by serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) (Linn et al., 2001).
source: This rate-limiting step in de novo synthesis of ceramide is catalyzed by serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) (Linn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Linn et al., 2001).

claim: Ceramide synthesis requires a reaction catalyzed by ceramide synthase (Mullen et al., 2012).
source: Ceramide synthesis also requires a reaction catalyzed by ceramide synthase (Mullen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Mullen et al., 2012).

claim: Treatment with doxorubicin increased the amount of [14C]palmitate incorporated into ceramide in Huh7 cells.
source: We confirmed that doxorubicin stimulated ceramide synthesis by showing that treatment with the compound increased the amount of [14C]palmitate incorporated into ceramide in Huh7 cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by radiolabeling data in Figure 6A.

claim: Doxorubicin primarily increased the amount of ceramide containing palmitate (16:0) as the amide-linked fatty acid.
source: Mass spectroscopy analysis revealed that doxorubicin primarily increased the amount of ceramide containing palmitate (16:0) as the amide-linked fatty acid (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by LC-MS data in Figure 6B.

claim: Etoposide failed to induce ceramide synthesis at a concentration at which cell proliferation was inhibited.
source: In contrast to doxorubicin, etoposide failed to induce ceramide synthesis at a concentration at which cell proliferation was inhibited (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown by radiolabeling data in Figure 6C.

claim: Treatment with myriocin inhibited doxorubicin-induced cleavage of CREB3L1.
source: To determine whether doxorubicin-induced ceramide synthesis is required to stimulate cleavage of CREB3L1, we treated Huh7 cells with myriocin, an inhibitor of SPT (Miyake et al., 1995). This treatment inhibited doxorubicin-induced cleavage of CREB3L1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 7A.

claim: Myriocin is an inhibitor of SPT (Miyake et al., 1995).
source: To determine whether doxorubicin-induced ceramide synthesis is required to stimulate cleavage of CREB3L1, we treated Huh7 cells with myriocin, an inhibitor of SPT (Miyake et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Miyake et al., 1995).

claim: Co-treatment with myriocin rendered Huh7 cells more resistant to doxorubicin.
source: Co-treatment with myriocin rendered the cells more resistant to doxorubicin (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown by cell proliferation data in Figure 7B.

claim: Fumonisin B1 is an inhibitor of ceramide synthase (Wang et al., 1991).
